query: For high-entropy-alloy protective coatings in wear-resistant applications, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs their wear performance and why? Define a controlled change that would distinguish the hypothesis from a baseline, the directional observations expected if it is correct, the range over which it should hold, the prior evidence that supports it, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Increasing the nanoscale grain boundary density in HEA protective coatings enhances wear resistance by promoting rapid and robust formation of a shear-induced and oxidation-accelerated protective tribolayer during sliding.
generation.material_initial_state: HEA protective coatings with a typical multiphase microstructure and moderate grain size, produced under standard deposition conditions.
generation.intervention: Adjust the processing parameters (e.g., deposition conditions or controlled thermal annealing) to refine the grain size and thereby increase the nanoscale grain boundary density while keeping the overall alloy composition constant.
generation.conditions: Wear testing under controlled sliding contact using industrially relevant loads, speeds, and temperatures (from room temperature up to moderately elevated temperatures) that simulate actual wear environments.
generation.structural_mediator: An increased density of nanoscale grain boundaries that act as active sites for localized shear, oxidation, and tribolayer nucleation.
generation.mechanism: The greater grain boundary area accelerates local shear and oxidation reactions, leading to the rapid formation of a continuous and protective oxide tribolayer (such as a spinel or chromia layer) during sliding. This tribolayer minimizes direct metal-to-metal contact and reduces friction, resulting in lower wear rates.
generation.predicted_outcome: Coatings with a higher grain boundary density will show a thicker and more uniform protective tribolayer, accompanied by lower wear rates and reduced coefficients of friction relative to baseline coatings with coarser grains.
generation.baseline: HEA coatings produced under standard processing conditions that yield coarser grains with lower grain boundary density, demonstrating less effective tribolayer formation and inferior wear resistance.
generation.boundary: The mechanistic effect is expected within the range of sliding loads, speeds, and temperatures typical for industrial wear applications. However, at extremes (very high temperatures or loads that induce different wear mechanisms or alter the coating composition), the hypothesized effect may not hold.
generation.uncertainty: While prior studies support enhanced oxidation and tribolayer formation with ultrafine grain structures, quantitative aspects such as the precise optimal grain size and the magnitude of improvement in wear resistance remain uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA coatings with identical alloy compositions and thicknesses. The first set (baseline) is produced under standard deposition conditions yielding coarser grains, while the second set is processed (via controlled thermal annealing or modified deposition parameters) to achieve nanocrystalline structures with a higher grain boundary density. Subject both sets to identical sliding wear tests under controlled load, speed, and temperature conditions.
measurements: Cross-sectional SEM/TEM and EDS mapping to quantify tribolayer thickness and uniformity
Tribometer-based wear rate measurements (material loss per distance or force unit)
In situ coefficient of friction recordings during wear tests
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the samples with increased grain boundary density fail to exhibit a statistically significant increase in the formation, continuity, or protective quality of the tribolayer, and no measurable reduction in wear rate or friction coefficient is observed compared to the baseline samples, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Development of high-entropy alloy (HEA) films is a promising and cost-effective way to incorporate these materials of superior properties in harsh environments. In this work, a refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) film of equimolar CuMoTaWV was deposited on silicon and 304 stainless-steel substrates using DC-magnetron sputtering. A sputtering target was developed by partial sintering of an equimolar powder mixture of Cu, Mo, Ta, W, and V using spark plasma sintering. The target was used to sputter a nanocrystalline RHEA film with a thickness of ∼900 nm and an average grain size of 18 nm. X-ray diffraction of the film revealed a body-centered cubic solid solution with preferred orientation in the (110) directional plane. The nanocrystalline nature of the RHEA film resulted in a hardness of 19 ± 2.3 GPa and an elastic modulus of 259 ± 19.2 GPa. Abstract In this study, the wear behaviour of a powder metallurgically produced AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 high-entropy alloy (HEAs) is investigated at elevated temperatures. Spark plasma sintering (SPS) of inert gas atomised feedstock enables the production of dense bulk material. The microstructure evolution and phase formation are analysed. The high cooling rate in the atomisation process results in spherical powder with a microstructure comprising two finely distributed body-centred cubic phases. An additional phase with a complex crystal structure precipitates during SPS processing, while no coarsening of microstructural features occurs. The wear resistance under reciprocating wear conditions increases at elevated temperatures due to the formation of a protective oxide layer under atmospherical conditions. Additionally, the coefficient of friction (COF) slightly decreases with increasing temperature. SPS processing is suitable for the production of HEA bulk material. An increase in the wear resistance at elevated temperature enables high temperature applications of the HEA system AlCoCrFeNiTi 0.5 . Abstract This work investigates the effect of ultrafine-grain microstructure on the oxidation behavior of AlCoCrFeNi high entropy alloy (HEA). The ultrafine-grain microstructure is obtained using stationary friction processing performed at two different rotational speeds, 400 and 1800 rpm, for 5 min duration. Processed samples demonstrate high depth of refinement (DOR) and ultrafine grain size (0.43–1 μm) at high rotational speeds along with significant phase transformations from BCC/B2 to FCC microstructure. Further, surface free energy of the ultrafine-grain microstructure is enhanced up to 35%. Oxidation kinetics of the ultrafine-grained sample is decelerated up to 12–48% in a temperature range of 850–1050 °C for a duration of 100 h. Chromia and alumina were the predominant oxides formed in almost all the samples oxidized at elevated temperature. In addition, spinel Co(Cr,Fe) 2 O 4 /Fe(Co,Cr) 2 O 4 formation is also detected in the unprocessed oxidized samples. Processed samples rich in grain boundaries (GBs) promote internal oxidation to form Al-rich inner oxides. frame.system: High-entropy alloy (HEA) protective coatings produced for wear-resistant applications, typically consisting of multi-principal element systems with complex phase and microstructural features (e.g., nanocrystalline or multiphase microstructures).
frame.goal: To identify and mechanistically explain which specific microstructural factor governs wear performance in HEA coatings, thereby predicting when and why their wear resistance is optimized under sliding conditions.
frame.limitation: There is currently no single, testable mechanistic model that directly links the complex microstructure of HEAs to their observed wear performance, making it difficult to predict and optimize their behavior under real-world wear conditions.

constraints: The hypothesis must be testable with a controlled change relative to a baseline sample
It must specify the expected directional changes in wear performance when one particular microstructural feature (or property) is intentionally altered
It should define the operational range (e.g., load, sliding speed, temperature) over which the hypothesis holds
Prior evidence supporting the mechanistic link must be referenced
A specific observation is required that would falsify the hypothesis if it were not met
frame.regime: Wear testing under sliding contact conditions with controlled load, speed, and temperature analogous to real application scenarios (e.g., conditions representing industrial wear environments).
prior_attempts: Previous studies have correlated high hardness, multiphase distributions, or high grain boundary densities with improved wear resistance in HEAs, but such correlations have not isolated a singular mechanism.

Attempts to link overall composition or simple hardness metrics to wear performance have fallen short because they did not account for dynamic processes like shear band formation or local plasticity changes during wear.

decision.trend: Early work on HEA coatings for wear performance has mostly reported correlations between global mechanical properties (e.g., hardness) and complex multiphase microstructures with improved wear behavior. For instance, PMC7515071 showed that under elevated temperature sliding the formation of a spinel (oxide) tribolayer accompanied a marked reduction in wear depth. Later, PMC7304825 extended this approach by synthesizing nanocrystalline RHEA films that demonstrated superior adhesion and reduced friction, hinting that nanoscale features (e.g., high grain boundary density and phase distributions) critically influence dynamic surface reactions during wear. Although these studies have modified processing routes to achieve desirable microstructures, they did not isolate one singular microstructural mechanism that directly governs the dynamic formation and stability of protective tribolayers under sliding conditions.
decision.unsolved: It remains unresolved which specific microstructural feature – for example, a high density of grain boundaries or the nature and fraction of nano/micro-scale phase interfaces – is the key controllable lever that triggers the formation of a stable, shear-induced tribolayer during wear testing. This open question impedes the establishment of a single, testable mechanistic model linking microstructural design to wear performance over an operational range (controlled load, sliding speed, and temperature).
decision.lever: Systematic tuning of the nanoscale grain boundary density via controlled thermal annealing or deposition conditions while keeping overall alloy composition unchanged
decision.why: Because earlier work indicates that the formation of protective oxide (spinel) tribolayers – and hence improved wear resistance – may be promoted by microstructures with high grain boundary or interface densities. By varying the grain size (and concomitantly the grain boundary area) in otherwise identical HEA coatings, one can directly test the hypothesis that an increased density of nanoscale interfaces facilitates a more robust, shear-induced tribolayer formation during sliding. This controlled-variable approach addresses the gap by isolating the microstructural parameter that governs the wear performance mechanistically.
